html:
A Muslim state ruled from Delhi that held much of north India, and at times the south, from 1206 to 1526. Five dynasties of Turkish and Afghan origin followed one another on its throne.

It grew from the conquests of Muhammad of Ghor, who defeated the Rajput king Prithviraj Chauhan in 1192. When Muhammad was killed in 1206, his slave general Qutb al-Din Aibak made himself sultan at Delhi and began the Qutb Minar.

The five dynasties:

  • Mamluk, or Slave, dynasty (1206 to 1290). Iltutmish secured the state; his daughter Razia ruled briefly as sultan.
  • Khalji (1290 to 1320). Alauddin Khalji beat back repeated Mongol invasions, fixed prices in Delhi's markets, and sent armies raiding deep into the south.
  • Tughlaq (1320 to 1414). Muhammad bin Tughluq moved the capital to Daulatabad in the Deccan and back, and tried a copper token currency that failed. The traveller Ibn Battuta served him as a judge. In 1398 Timur sacked Delhi.
  • Sayyid (1414 to 1451). A weak state around Delhi.
  • Lodi (1451 to 1526). Afghan rulers who revived it, until Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat.

The sultanate kept north India largely safe from the Mongols. It also built a new Indo-Islamic culture: mosques and tombs mixing Persian and Indian styles, Persian as the language of government, and the beginnings of Urdu. In the 14th century the south broke away, into the Bahmani sultanate and the Hindu kingdom of Vijayanagara.
sum: A Muslim state ruled from Delhi that held much of north India, and at times the south, from 1206 to 1526. Five dynasties of Turkish and Afghan origin followed one another on its throne.
